claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) imports and metabolizes fatty acids to maintain infection within human macrophages.
source: Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) imports and metabolizes fatty acids to maintain infection within human macrophages.
evidence: This is stated as an established paradigm in the abstract, drawing from established scientific consensus.

claim: LucA and Mce1 are required for fatty acid import in Mtb.
source: Previously, we found that LucA and Mce1 are required for fatty acid import in Mtb (Nazarova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to previous work (Nazarova et al., 2017).

claim: rv2799 is necessary for fatty acid import in Mtb during infection within macrophages.
source: This screen identified the novel genes as rv2799 and rv0966c as be necessary for fatty acid import and confirmed the central role for Rv3723/LucA and putative components of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter (Rv0200/OmamB, Rv0172/Mce1D, and Rv0655/MceG) in this process.
evidence: Identified through the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: rv0966c is necessary for fatty acid import in Mtb during infection within macrophages.
source: This screen identified the novel genes as rv2799 and rv0966c as be necessary for fatty acid import and confirmed the central role for Rv3723/LucA and putative components of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter (Rv0200/OmamB, Rv0172/Mce1D, and Rv0655/MceG) in this process.
evidence: Identified through the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Rv3723/LucA plays a central role in fatty acid import in Mtb.
source: This screen identified the novel genes as rv2799 and rv0966c as be necessary for fatty acid import and confirmed the central role for Rv3723/LucA and putative components of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter (Rv0200/OmamB, Rv0172/Mce1D, and Rv0655/MceG) in this process.
evidence: Confirmed through the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Rv0200/OmamB is a putative component of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter necessary for fatty acid import.
source: This screen identified the novel genes as rv2799 and rv0966c as be necessary for fatty acid import and confirmed the central role for Rv3723/LucA and putative components of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter (Rv0200/OmamB, Rv0172/Mce1D, and Rv0655/MceG) in this process.
evidence: Confirmed through the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Rv0172/Mce1D is a putative component of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter necessary for fatty acid import.
source: This screen identified the novel genes as rv2799 and rv0966c as be necessary for fatty acid import and confirmed the central role for Rv3723/LucA and putative components of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter (Rv0200/OmamB, Rv0172/Mce1D, and Rv0655/MceG) in this process.
evidence: Confirmed through the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Rv0655/MceG is a putative component of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter necessary for fatty acid import.
source: This screen identified the novel genes as rv2799 and rv0966c as be necessary for fatty acid import and confirmed the central role for Rv3723/LucA and putative components of the Mce1 fatty acid transporter (Rv0200/OmamB, Rv0172/Mce1D, and Rv0655/MceG) in this process.
evidence: Confirmed through the genetic screen described in the manuscript.

claim: Mycobacterium tuberculosis isolated from mouse lungs preferentially metabolizes fatty acids ex vivo.
source: Early studies established that Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) isolated from mouse lungs preferentially metabolizes fatty acids ex vivo (Bloch and SEGAL, 1956).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bloch and SEGAL, 1956.

claim: Mtb upregulates genes needed for fatty acid utilization during infection in macrophages.
source: It is known that Mtb upregulates genes needed for fatty acid utilization during infection in macrophages, mouse challenge models, and within human lung tissues (Fontán et al., 2008; Homolka et al., 2010; Rachman et al., 2006; Rohde et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2012; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Tailleux et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Fontán et al., 2008; Homolka et al., 2010; Rachman et al., 2006; Rohde et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2012; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Tailleux et al., 2008).

claim: Mtb upregulates genes needed for fatty acid utilization during mouse challenge models.
source: It is known that Mtb upregulates genes needed for fatty acid utilization during infection in macrophages, mouse challenge models, and within human lung tissues (Fontán et al., 2008; Homolka et al., 2010; Rachman et al., 2006; Rohde et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2012; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Tailleux et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Fontán et al., 2008; Homolka et al., 2010; Rachman et al., 2006; Rohde et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2012; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Tailleux et al., 2008).

claim: Mtb upregulates genes needed for fatty acid utilization within human lung tissues.
source: It is known that Mtb upregulates genes needed for fatty acid utilization during infection in macrophages, mouse challenge models, and within human lung tissues (Fontán et al., 2008; Homolka et al., 2010; Rachman et al., 2006; Rohde et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2012; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Tailleux et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations (Fontán et al., 2008; Homolka et al., 2010; Rachman et al., 2006; Rohde et al., 2007; Rohde et al., 2012; Schnappinger et al., 2003; Tailleux et al., 2008).

claim: Mtb can import and metabolize fatty acids.
source: Functional experiments have also established that Mtb can import and metabolize fatty acids (Lee et al., 2013) or the acyl-chains derived from triacylglycerol (Daniel et al., 2011), and fluorescent fatty acid trafficking studies have visualized the presence of lipid inclusions in intracellular Mtb (Podinovskaia et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee et al., 2013.

claim: Mtb can import and metabolize acyl-chains derived from triacylglycerol.
source: Functional experiments have also established that Mtb can import and metabolize fatty acids (Lee et al., 2013) or the acyl-chains derived from triacylglycerol (Daniel et al., 2011), and fluorescent fatty acid trafficking studies have visualized the presence of lipid inclusions in intracellular Mtb (Podinovskaia et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Daniel et al., 2011.

claim: Fluorescent fatty acid trafficking studies have visualized the presence of lipid inclusions in intracellular Mtb.
source: Functional experiments have also established that Mtb can import and metabolize fatty acids (Lee et al., 2013) or the acyl-chains derived from triacylglycerol (Daniel et al., 2011), and fluorescent fatty acid trafficking studies have visualized the presence of lipid inclusions in intracellular Mtb (Podinovskaia et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Podinovskaia et al., 2013.

claim: Intracellular Mtb resides in foamy macrophages in human granulomatous lesions.
source: In human granulomatous lesions, intracellular Mtb resides in foamy macrophages (Peyron et al., 2008) and these cells are known to concentrate triacylglycerol, cholesterol, and cholesterol esters (Almeida et al., 2012; McClean and Tobin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Peyron et al., 2008.

claim: Foamy macrophages concentrate triacylglycerol, cholesterol, and cholesterol esters.
source: In human granulomatous lesions, intracellular Mtb resides in foamy macrophages (Peyron et al., 2008) and these cells are known to concentrate triacylglycerol, cholesterol, and cholesterol esters (Almeida et al., 2012; McClean and Tobin, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Almeida et al., 2012 and McClean and Tobin, 2016.

claim: The caseous centers of necrotic TB lesions are enriched in triacylglycerol, cholesterol, and cholesterol esters.
source: Additionally, the caseous centers of necrotic TB lesions are enriched in these same lipids and extracellular bacteria are commonly found embedded in this nutrient-rich material (Cáceres et al., 2009; Hunter et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cáceres et al., 2009; Hunter et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Extracellular bacteria are commonly found embedded in the caseous centers of necrotic TB lesions.
source: Additionally, the caseous centers of necrotic TB lesions are enriched in these same lipids and extracellular bacteria are commonly found embedded in this nutrient-rich material (Cáceres et al., 2009; Hunter et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cáceres et al., 2009; Hunter et al., 2007; Kim et al., 2010.

claim: Rv3723/LucA is required for fatty acid import in Mtb.
source: Although the principles of fatty acid uptake in Mtb are poorly understood, we recently discovered that Rv3723/LucA and the Mce1 transporter complex are required for fatty acid import (Nazarova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: The Mce1 transporter complex is required for fatty acid import in Mtb.
source: Although the principles of fatty acid uptake in Mtb are poorly understood, we recently discovered that Rv3723/LucA and the Mce1 transporter complex are required for fatty acid import (Nazarova et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: Rv3723/LucA and Mce1 are needed for full Mtb virulence in murine infection models.
source: Given that these proteins are needed for full Mtb virulence in murine infection models (Joshi et al., 2006; Nazarova et al., 2017), we sought to identify additional genes that are involved in this process.
evidence: Supported by citations to Joshi et al., 2006 and Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: Rv3723/LucA is required for both fatty acid and cholesterol import in Mtb.
source: Rv3723/LucA is required for both fatty acid and cholesterol import in Mtb (Nazarova et al., 2017), and we have demonstrated that a robust phenotype of a Mtb mutant lacking Rv3723/LucA (∆lucA::hyg) is the inability of this strain to import the fluorescent fatty acid substrate, Bodipy-palmitate during infection in macrophages.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: A Mtb mutant lacking Rv3723/LucA (∆lucA::hyg) is unable to import Bodipy-palmitate during infection in macrophages.
source: Rv3723/LucA is required for both fatty acid and cholesterol import in Mtb (Nazarova et al., 2017), and we have demonstrated that a robust phenotype of a Mtb mutant lacking Rv3723/LucA (∆lucA::hyg) is the inability of this strain to import the fluorescent fatty acid substrate, Bodipy-palmitate during infection in macrophages.
evidence: Demonstrated by the authors in previous work.

claim: The ∆lucA::hyg mutant incorporated less Bodipy-palmitate relative to WT.
source: Applying this sorting strategy to the ∆lucA::hyg mutant confirmed that this strain incorporated less Bodipy-palmitate relative to WT (Figure 1D).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 98.68 ± 1.31% of the sorted Bodipy-low population were hygromycin-resistant ∆lucA::hyg bacteria.
source: Of the sorted cells in the desired Bodipy-low population 98.68 ± 1.31% of the recovered colonies were hygromycin-resistant, demonstrating that the majority of sorted population were indeed ∆lucA::hyg bacteria indicating the high degree of specificity with this approach.
evidence: Quantified by plating on selective agar.

claim: A transposon mutant library of approximately 2×10^4 mutants was generated in Mtb Erdman strain.
source: Using the MycoMarT7 transposon (Sassetti et al., 2001) delivered by phage transduction (Bardarov et al., 1997), we generated a transposon mutant library (~2×104 mutants) in a Mtb Erdman strain which expresses mCherry from a chromosomally integrated plasmid (Stover et al., 1991).
evidence: Described in the methods and results of the manuscript.

claim: Of the 10^5 events collected in the Bodipy-low sort, only ~12.8% gave rise to colonies.
source: Of the 105 events collected in the Bodipy-low sort, only ~12.8% (~1.28×104) gave rise to colonies.
evidence: Quantified from the sorting experiment.

claim: When the Bodipy-low population was sorted from the 1:1 mixture containing WT and ∆lucA::hyg strains, ~71.9 ± 0.67% of the sorted events produced colonies.
source: For comparison, when the Bodipy-low population was sorted from the 1:1 mixture containing WT and ∆lucA::hyg strains ~ 71.9 ± 0.67% of the sorted events produced colonies.
evidence: Quantified from the sorting experiment.

claim: A large proportion (~60%) of the clones in the Bodipy-low population are non-viable or non-culturable with the plating conditions used.
source: The reduced recovery of mutant bacteria from the Bodipy-low population suggests that a large proportion (~60%) of the clones are non-viable or non-culturable with our plating conditions.
evidence: Inferred from the difference in colony recovery rates between the mutant library and the control mixture.

claim: Following the second enrichment sort, ~5.3×10^4 (53%) of the Bodipy-low population yielded viable colonies.
source: Following the second enrichment sort, 105 Bodipy-low events were collected, and ~5.3×104 (53%) of this population yielded viable colonies.
evidence: Quantified from the sorting experiment.

claim: Each round of selection enriched for mutants with a decreased ability to incorporate Bodipy-palmitate.
source: Each round of selection enriched for mutants with a decreased ability to incorporate Bodipy-palmitate (Figure 2A).
evidence: Demonstrated by flow analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The TraSH analysis identified 73 insertion sites that map to 65 genes or intragenic regions with a fivefold overrepresentation with p-value < 0.05 after the second enrichment sort.
source: Our analysis of the mutants isolated from the second enrichment sort identified 73 insertion sites that map to 65 genes or intragenic regions with a fivefold overrepresentation with p-value < 0.05 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Determined by TraSH analysis of the sorted mutant pools.

claim: Transposon mutations in rv3723/lucA are overrepresented 13.67-fold (p = 1.24 × 10^-11) following the second round of enrichment.
source: Importantly, our selection strategy also confirmed that transposon mutations in rv3723/lucA are overrepresented following the second round of enrichment (13.67-fold overrepresented, p = 1.24 × 10−11) (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Determined by TraSH analysis shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Thirty-seven of the 46 clones (80%) isolated in the second round of selection contained insertions in the same genes as mapped by TraSH (>5 fold overrepresentation; p < 0.05).
source: Thirty-seven of the 46 clones (80%) isolated in the second round of selection contained insertions in the same genes as mapped by TraSH (>5 fold overrepresentation; p < 0.05) revealing a significant correlation in the dataset (Figure 2B and Figure 2—source data 2).
evidence: Determined by DNA sequencing of individual clones and comparison to TraSH data.

claim: Six of the 13 tested mutants were defective in Bodipy-palmitate import at levels less than 50%.
source: This analysis determined that 6 of the 13 mutants were defective in Bodipy-palmitate import at levels less than 50%.
evidence: Quantified by flow cytometry during macrophage infection.

claim: The six mutants with the strongest defect in Bodipy-palmitate uptake by flow cytometry also showed reduced uptake by confocal microscopy.
source: This flow cytometric analysis was confirmed by confocal microscopy demonstrating that the same six mutants have the strongest defect in Bodipy-palmitate uptake within macrophages (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Confirmed by confocal microscopy shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Mutants defective in fatty acid import during infection in macrophages that demonstrated a pronounced reduction in 14C-fatty acid metabolism had transposon insertions in genes encoded within the mce1 operon (rv0172/mce1D) or in genes encoding proteins believed to be part of the Mce1 transporter (rv0655/mceG, rv0200/omamB).
source: Mutants defective in fatty acid import during infection in macrophages that demonstrated a pronounced reduction in 14C-fatty acid metabolism had transposon insertions in genes encoded within the mce1 operon (rv0172/mce1D) or in genes encoding proteins believed to be part of the Mce1 transporter (rv0655/mceG, rv0200/omamB) (Joshi et al., 2006; Perkowski et al., 2016) indicating an important role for these genes and Mce1 complex in the import and/or metabolism of fatty acids.
evidence: Determined by fatty acid metabolism assays and supported by citations to Joshi et al., 2006 and Perkowski et al., 2016.

claim: A mutant with transposon insertion in rv0966c has a reduced ability to import Bodipy-palmitate in macrophages (~85% reduction) and a decreased ability to metabolize 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~60% reduction).
source: A mutant with transposon insertion in rv0966c, a gene of unknown function also has both a reduced ability to import Bodipy-palmitate in macrophages (~85% reduction) and a decreased ability to metabolize 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~60% reduction) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantified by flow cytometry and radiorespirometry assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A mutant with a transposon insertion within the mce1 operon (rv0175/mam1A) has a minor defect in Bodipy-palmitate import during infection in macrophages (~20% reduction) but has pronounced defect in metabolizing 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~98% reduction).
source: One mutant with a transposon insertion within the mce1 operon (rv0175/mam1A) has a minor defect in Bodipy-palmitate import during infection in macrophages (~20% reduction) but has pronounced defect in metabolizing 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~98% reduction) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantified by flow cytometry and radiorespirometry assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mutants with transposon insertions in rv2799 and rv2583c/relA have a decreased ability to import Bodipy-palmitate in macrophages (~55% and ~50% reduction, respectively) while both displayed an increase in the bacterium's ability to metabolize 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~35% and ~125% increase, respectively).
source: Mutants with transposon insertions in rv2799 and rv2583c/relA have a decreased ability to import Bodipy-palmitate in macrophages (~55% and~50% reduction, respectively) while both of these mutants displayed an increase in the bacterium's ability to metabolize 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~35% and~125% increase, respectively) (Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantified by flow cytometry and radiorespirometry assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: A rv3484/cpsA transposon mutant has a decreased ability to import Bodipy-palmitate in macrophages (~70% reduction), yet this mutant displayed a subtle decrease in the bacterium's ability to metabolize 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~20% decrease).
source: A rv3484/cpsA transposon mutant has a decreased ability to import Bodipy-palmitate in macrophages (~70% reduction), yet this mutant displayed a subtle decrease in the bacterium's ability to metabolize 14C-fatty acid in liquid culture (~20% decrease)
evidence: Quantified by flow cytometry and radiorespirometry assays.

claim: Transposon insertions in rv0200/OmamB, rv0172/mce1D, and rv0655/mceG had the most pronounced defect in fatty acid import.
source: Transposon insertions in rv0200/OmamB, rv0172/mce1D, and rv0655/mceG had the most pronounced defect in fatty acid import (Figure 3B).
evidence: Quantified by direct measurement of [1-14C]-oleate import shown in Figure 3B.

claim: rv0200/OmamB, rv0172/mce1D, rv0655/mceG, and rv0966c are involved in fatty acid import in liquid culture and during macrophage infection.
source: Together these data indicate that rv0200/OmamB, rv0172/mce1D, rv0655/mceG, and rv0966c are involved in fatty acid import in liquid culture and during macrophage infection.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of Bodipy-palmitate import and fatty acid metabolism assays.

claim: Transposon insertions in rv0175/mam1A, rv2799, rv2583c/relA, and rv3484/cpsA display condition-dependent reductions in the import and/or metabolism of fatty acids.
source: Alternatively, transposon insertions in rv0175/mam1A, rv2799, rv2583c/relA, and rv3484/cpsA display condition-dependent reductions in the import and/or metabolism of fatty acids (Figure 3A).
evidence: Inferred from the differential phenotypes observed in macrophage infection versus axenic culture shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Mce1 is a dedicated fatty acid transporter.
source: Specifically, we proposed that Mce1 is a dedicated fatty acid transporter and LucA is a shared protein which interacts with Mce1 and Mce4 subunits to facilitate Mce1- and Mce4-mediated import of fatty acids and cholesterol, respectively (Nazarova et al., 2017).
evidence: Proposed model supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: LucA is a shared protein which interacts with Mce1 and Mce4 subunits to facilitate Mce1- and Mce4-mediated import of fatty acids and cholesterol, respectively.
source: Specifically, we proposed that Mce1 is a dedicated fatty acid transporter and LucA is a shared protein which interacts with Mce1 and Mce4 subunits to facilitate Mce1- and Mce4-mediated import of fatty acids and cholesterol, respectively (Nazarova et al., 2017).
evidence: Proposed model supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: The link between LucA and the Mce1/Mce4 transporters suggests that fatty acid and cholesterol import is coordinated in Mtb.
source: The link between LucA and the Mce1/Mce4 transporters suggests that fatty acid and cholesterol import is coordinated in Mtb and this may reflect the abundance of fatty acids and cholesterol within the macrophage niche.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the relationship between LucA and Mce transporters.

claim: The coordination of fatty acid and cholesterol import may reflect the abundance of fatty acids and cholesterol within the macrophage niche.
source: The link between LucA and the Mce1/Mce4 transporters suggests that fatty acid and cholesterol import is coordinated in Mtb and this may reflect the abundance of fatty acids and cholesterol within the macrophage niche.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the biological significance.

claim: The TraSH-based analyses identified six total genes in the mce1 operon that were overrepresented following the enrichment screen (rv0168/yrbE1B, rv0169/mce1A, rv0171/mce1C, rv0172/mce1D, rv0175/mam1A, and rv0176/mam1B).
source: Our TraSH-based analyses also identified six total genes in the mce1 operon that were overrepresented following the enrichment screen (rv0168/yrbE1B, rv0169/mce1A, rv0171/mce1C, rv0172/mce1D, rv0175/mam1A, and rv0176/mam1B (Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Determined by TraSH analysis.

claim: Mutations in genes encoding the orphaned Mce accessory subunits (rv0199/omamA and rv0200/omamB) were overrepresented in the enrichment screen.
source: This analysis also revealed that mutations in genes encoding the orphaned Mce accessory subunits (rv0199/omamA and rv0200/omamB) were overrepresented in our enrichment screen.
evidence: Determined by TraSH analysis.

claim: Rv0199/OmamA is known to interact with Rv3723/LucA.
source: The accessory subunit, Rv0199/OmamA is known to interact with Rv3723/LucA (Nazarova et al., 2017) and to stabilize the Mce1 complex (Perkowski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nazarova et al., 2017.

claim: Rv0199/OmamA stabilizes the Mce1 complex.
source: The accessory subunit, Rv0199/OmamA is known to interact with Rv3723/LucA (Nazarova et al., 2017) and to stabilize the Mce1 complex (Perkowski et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Perkowski et al., 2016.

claim: It is possible that OmamB and OmamA function jointly to stabilize Mce1 through interactions with Rv3723/LucA.
source: It is possible that OmamB and OmamA function jointly to stabilize Mce1 through interactions with Rv3723/LucA.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the known function of OmamA.

claim: It has long been hypothesized that the putative ATPase, Rv0655/MceG provides energy for all Mce transporters in Mtb.
source: It has long been hypothesized that the putative ATPase, Rv0655/MceG provides energy for all Mce transporters in Mtb (Joshi et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citation to Joshi et al., 2006.

claim: Rv0655/MceG has been shown to be required for cholesterol metabolism in Mtb.
source: Rv0655/MceG has been shown to be required for cholesterol metabolism in Mtb (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008), and however, in Mycobacterium smegmatis (García-Fernández et al., 2017), its role in fatty acid assimilation had not been described previously.
evidence: Supported by citation to Pandey and Sassetti, 2008.

claim: The role of Rv0655/MceG in fatty acid assimilation had not been described previously in Mycobacterium smegmatis.
source: Rv0655/MceG has been shown to be required for cholesterol metabolism in Mtb (Pandey and Sassetti, 2008), and however, in Mycobacterium smegmatis (García-Fernández et al., 2017), its role in fatty acid assimilation had not been described previously.
evidence: Supported by citation to García-Fernández et al., 2017.

claim: Among the mutants tested, rv0655/mceG had the strongest defect in fatty acid import and metabolism (comparable to rv3723/lucA).
source: Among the mutants tested here rv0655/mceG had the strongest defect in fatty acid import and metabolism (comparable to rv3723/lucA), supporting its essential role in these processes (Figure 3).
evidence: Quantified by fatty acid import and metabolism assays shown in Figure 3.

claim: Mce1 functions as a fatty acid transporter within the macrophage environment.
source: Thus, given that we identified a number of Mce1 subunits in the screen, we conclude that Mce1 functions as a fatty acid transporter within the macrophage environment (Figure 3C).
evidence: Inferred from the identification of multiple Mce1 subunits in the screen.

claim: The putative protein encoded by rv0966 contains a domain of unknown function (DUF1707) that is commonly found in proteins from Actinomycetal species.
source: The putative protein encoded by rv0966 contains a domain of unknown function (DUF1707) that is commonly found in proteins from Actinomycetal species.
evidence: Based on bioinformatic analysis of the protein sequence.

claim: The gene rv0966c is highly expressed in a mouse infection model.
source: The gene rv0966c is highly expressed in a mouse infection model (Talaat et al., 2007) but more work will be needed to determine how Rv0966c facilitates fatty acids import in Mtb.
evidence: Supported by citation to Talaat et al., 2007.

claim: Inactivation of Rv2583c/RelA dramatically increases fatty acid metabolism in Mtb.
source: Inactivation of Rv2583c/RelA dramatically increases fatty acid metabolism in Mtb, yet this mutant imports less Bodipy-palmitate during macrophage infection (Figure 3A).
evidence: Quantified by fatty acid metabolism assays shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Rv2583c/RelA mediates the stringent response following nutrient deprivation by regulating levels of (p)ppGpp.
source: Rv2583c/RelA mediates the stringent response following nutrient deprivation by regulating levels of (p)ppGpp (Avarbock et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Avarbock et al., 1999.

claim: RelA is required for long-term survival of Mtb in vitro and in vivo.
source: RelA is required for long-term survival of Mtb in vitro and in vivo; however, deletion of RelA is reported to have no effect on Mtb growth during short-term macrophage infections (Dahl et al., 2003; Klinkenberg et al., 2010; Primm et al., 2000; Weiss and Stallings, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dahl et al., 2003; Klinkenberg et al., 2010; Primm et al., 2000; Weiss and Stallings, 2013.

claim: Deletion of RelA is reported to have no effect on Mtb growth during short-term macrophage infections.
source: RelA is required for long-term survival of Mtb in vitro and in vivo; however, deletion of RelA is reported to have no effect on Mtb growth during short-term macrophage infections (Dahl et al., 2003; Klinkenberg et al., 2010; Primm et al., 2000; Weiss and Stallings, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Dahl et al., 2003; Klinkenberg et al., 2010; Primm et al., 2000; Weiss and Stallings, 2013.

claim: Inactivation of RelA decreases the expression of mce1, mce3 and mce4 operons in response to starvation.
source: Inactivation of RelA decreases the expression of mce1, mce3 and mce4 operons in response to starvation (Dahl et al., 2003), suggesting that Rv2583c/RelA might be involved in the regulating lipid import in an environment-dependent manner.
evidence: Supported by citation to Dahl et al., 2003.

claim: Rv2583c/RelA might be involved in regulating lipid import in an environment-dependent manner.
source: Inactivation of RelA decreases the expression of mce1, mce3 and mce4 operons in response to starvation (Dahl et al., 2003), suggesting that Rv2583c/RelA might be involved in the regulating lipid import in an environment-dependent manner.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the effect of RelA on mce operon expression.

claim: The CpsA (capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis) protein participates in the ligation of arabinogalactan to peptidoglycan in the Mtb cell wall.
source: The CpsA (capsular polysaccharide biosynthesis) protein participates in the ligation of arabinogalactan to peptidoglycan in the Mtb cell wall (Grzegorzewicz et al., 2016; Harrison et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grzegorzewicz et al., 2016 and Harrison et al., 2016.

claim: Within macrophages, bacteria lacking CpsA fail to block LC3-associated lysosomal trafficking.
source: Within macrophages, bacteria lacking CpsA also fail to block LC3-associated lysosomal trafficking, instead these bacteria traffic into NADPH-oxidase-positive phagosomes for clearance by the host cell (Köster et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Köster et al., 2017.

claim: Bacteria lacking CpsA traffic into NADPH-oxidase-positive phagosomes for clearance by the host cell.
source: Within macrophages, bacteria lacking CpsA also fail to block LC3-associated lysosomal trafficking, instead these bacteria traffic into NADPH-oxidase-positive phagosomes for clearance by the host cell (Köster et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Köster et al., 2017.

claim: It is possible that the CpsA mutant's defect in Bodipy-palmitate import in macrophages may be due to perturbations in the bacterial cell wall, intracellular trafficking and/or a decrease in bacterial viability.
source: Thus, it is possible that the CpsA mutant's defect in Bodipy-palmitate import in macrophages may be due perturbations in the bacterial cell wall, intracellular trafficking and/or a decrease in bacterial viability.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the CpsA mutant phenotype.

claim: A balanced utilization of cholesterol and fatty acids is significant for Mtb fitness, growth and virulence.
source: Although we focused on fatty acid import here, it is understood that a balanced utilization of cholesterol and fatty acids is significant for Mtb fitness, growth and virulence (Lee et al., 2013; Nazarova et al., 2017; Wilburn et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lee et al., 2013; Nazarova et al., 2017; Wilburn et al., 2018.

claim: Fatty acid and cholesterol import in Mtb are governed by a network of proteins that facilitate metabolic adaptations to various environmental pressures that the bacteria encounter during infection.
source: We hypothesize that fatty acid and cholesterol import in Mtb are governed by a network of proteins that facilitate metabolic adaptations to various environmental pressures that the bacteria encounter during infection (Huang et al., 2018).
evidence: Hypothesis supported by citation to Huang et al., 2018.

claim: Mtb's metabolism is constrained within macrophages.
source: Growing evidence indicates that Mtb's metabolism is constrained within macrophages (VanderVen et al., 2015) yet is integrated to the metabolism of host cells.
evidence: Supported by citation to VanderVen et al., 2015.

claim: Mtb's metabolism is integrated to the metabolism of host cells.
source: Growing evidence indicates that Mtb's metabolism is constrained within macrophages (VanderVen et al., 2015) yet is integrated to the metabolism of host cells.
evidence: Based on established scientific understanding.

claim: Understanding the complex process of lipid import in Mtb during infection may shed new light on weakness in the bacterial adaptation to host environment that can be targeted with antituberculosis therapies.
source: Thus, understanding the complex process of lipid import in Mtb during infection may shed new light on weakness in the bacterial adaptation to host environment that can be targeted with antituberculosis therapies.
evidence: Speculative statement about the potential therapeutic implications of the research.

claim: The sorted bacterial Bodipy-low population approached ~84% purity.
source: Flow analysis determined that sorted bacterial Bodipy-low population approached ~84% purity (Figure 1E).
evidence: Quantified by flow analysis shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Fatty acid import is mediated by a network of shared and dedicated proteins that import fatty acids via Mce transporter in Mtb.
source: Together these data support our previous findings and are consistent with the concept that fatty acid import in Mtb is mediated by a network of shared and dedicated proteins that import fatty acids via Mce transporter in Mtb.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of the genetic screen and phenotypic characterization.
